items.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 10, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: He was telling the musical story of what was happening. And that kind of like influenced me you know.

ctx.x: I’d like to get at an issue and start with a quote. The issue is the role of jazz in society and how society affects jazz. And this is a quote from Max Roach that was connected to the “We Insist Freedom Now” LP, it was 1962. And he said “We American jazz musicians of African descent have proved beyond all doubt that we’re master musicians of our instruments. Now what we have to do is employ our skill to tell the dramatic story of our people and what we’ve been through.” So my question to you is did that music…

I admired Max. Sun Ra was more influential in terms of he affected my direction more than Max. Trane did. I liked Mingus but everybody was doing the same — had the same purpose but different ways of approaching to try to play freer, trying to play freer. And this meant, in terms of changing the format, like for instance Horace Silver, he’d just play — Horace Silver was very popular. He was a business guy. And he’d play and wrote tunes that sold. He had his own publishing — he was one of the first black musicians…

Because I produced a record called “Evening with the Devil” in 1970 which had “Mary Had an Abortion.” This was “Mary Had an Abortion,” which was a poem. But the first one was written by myself, which was a reflection of Africa being Mary and having an abortion of a people, undeveloped people, and that was the first poem that was recited by me. And then I employed a group of actors, it was something like The Last Poets, which wrote a tune, “Mary Had an Abortion.”

items.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 17, 2022 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: John started using him on gigs

ctx.x: My spirituality. You know, so he had to wean me off of that foundation. And then I noticed a lot of guys, he was using a lot of musicians but he liked the guys that didn’t have that foundation so much. You know he gravitated to those guys because it was less work to re-indoctrinate you know. Same with John Coltrane. John Coltrane liked Pharoah because he hadn’t had the bebop foundation so much. Pharoah was like a blues kind of guy from Arkansas. And he was — me and Pharoah, he was a year older than me. He was a…

was hanging out with John Coltrane. John liked him you know. So he did more and more with John and John started using him on gigs and whatnot, and he started touring and whatnot, the rest is history. Now with Sun Ra I used to make fun of Sun Ra but something that I really took serious when I saw he was recording everything you know. Rehearsals. And he had two record labels. You know he was producing and marketing his music, and his music was in the marketplace. Of course it was like a small niche fan base. But it…
Homogenized is a good word. Can I ask if you recall on the live gigs you played if he attracted a mostly white audience or a mostly black audience?
